literal_meaning: Older sister / older brother (depends on your gender)

seo.meta_title: Calling an Older Korean Friend by Name? | 언니, 오빠, 형, 누나 Explained
seo.meta_description: AI keeps using a friend's first name in Korean, but calling an older friend by name can feel rude. Learn when to use 언니, 오빠, 형 and 누나.

ai_failure.situation: Texting a friend who is two years older than you: 'Jiwon, are you free tomorrow?'
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Outputs '지원아, 내일 시간 있어?' — the older friend's bare name plus casual speech, copying the English.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: Calling someone older by their bare name (with 아/야) is how you address equals or juniors. Even close friends usually call an older friend with a kinship title, and AI also mixes up which title matches whose gender.

natural_solution.rule: The title depends on BOTH your gender and theirs. Women say 언니 (older woman) and 오빠 (older man). Men say 누나 (older woman) and 형 (older man). Add the name for clarity: 지원 언니.

alternatives.context: A woman to an older female friend
A man to an older male friend he's close with
Older person from school or work you're not close to yet

nuance: Koreans establish relative age early in a relationship because it decides how people address each other. Kinship titles turn friends into a kind of chosen family and carry real warmth — 오빠 in particular can also sound affectionate or flirtatious, so context matters. Before you're close, 선배(님) or name + 씨 keeps a respectful distance. Moving to bare names usually happens only when the older person suggests it, often with 말 놓자 (let's drop the formal speech).
